Multi-omics has shifted from a methodological aspiration to a routine design choice in the life sciences. Simultaneous profiling of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic and microbial layers enables simultaneous interrogation of multi-layer microbial data, motivating recent calls for standardized, FAIR-compliant workflows [R54]. What has lagged behind this conceptual maturation, however, is the software infrastructure that researchers must actually use. In our assessment of the field, a typical multi-omics project now involves roughly five to seven data types and on the order of several thousand samples, with each analytical step admitting a dozen or more competing implementations; these figures are author estimates rather than findings cited from the literature. The tooling has accumulated faster than the standards that should govern it, and the result is an analytical gap that is no longer conceptual but infrastructural: researchers spend more time reconciling file formats, harmonizing object classes and reproducing someone else's R environment than they do interpreting biological signal.

The heterogeneity of the available tools is striking. On the R side, Bioconductor provides the foundational data structures, most notably MultiAssayExperiment, which offers coordinated representation, storage and operation on diverse genomics datasets and ships with ready-to-analyze TCGA objects [R28]; on top of this substrate the community has built package-specific integrators such as mixOmics with its DIABLO supervised framework [R27], the longitudinal timeOmics [R20] and netOmics packages [R21], the vertical and horizontal miodin workflow [R48], the MOFA-based transfer-learning extension MOTL [R32], the MuSA radiogenomic GUI built on the same MultiAssayExperiment class [R25], and reproducibility-oriented wrappers such as moiraine that preprocess data, run one or more integration methods and enable head-to-head comparison across integration tools [R3]. The Python ecosystem is no less crowded, ranging from graph-neural-network frameworks such as BioNeuralNet [R5] to specialised deep-learning integrators including MOADLN, which uses self-attention and a Multi-Omics Correlation Discovery Network to combine omics-specific encoders before classification [R17], MCluster-VAEs [R22], MO-GCAN [R29], DeepMoIC [R12] and MoAGL-SA [R39]. Parallel to these programmatic ecosystems, web-based point-and-click platforms have proliferated: the Analyst suite (ExpressAnalyst, MetaboAnalyst, OmicsNet, OmicsAnalyst) [R8], ExpOmics [R41], the single-cell analyst [R6], CFViSA, a free web platform integrating 79 tools with microbiome and transcriptome pipelines [R40], NOODAI [R33], PhenoMultiOmics [R14] and disease-specific portals such as CPMOAD [R7] and LOSTdb [R34] now offer GUI-driven alternatives that lower the barrier to entry but introduce their own concerns about transparency and reproducibility. Finally, containerised, workflow-management approaches — Nextflow, Snakemake and WorkflowHub-compatible Research Object Crates [R11, R26, R35] — attempt to capture provenance at the level of the analysis environment itself.

Among these application domains, host–microbiome research exemplifies the infrastructural pressure particularly acutely. Microbial community samples bring together metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics and metabolomics, with sample coverage that is intrinsically inconsistent across layers, reflecting taxa-specific differences in detectability [R1]. As the microbial multi-omics perspective of Van Den Bossche and colleagues emphasises, the complexity of analysing a single isolate is multiplied further when samples comprise hundreds to thousands of individual species, yet standardised workflows and benchmarked datasets remain scarce [R54]. This combination — heterogeneous data formats, inconsistent sample coverage, complex analytical chains and weak reproducibility standards — illustrates the kind of field-level bottleneck that workflow-level solutions such as EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) attempt to address. EMP is an R workflow built on SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment that organises extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation into a single coherent pipeline [R1]. Microbiome multi-omics is therefore not just another application area; it is a particularly demanding setting in which any claim that multi-omics infrastructure has matured is put to the test.

A candid assessment must temper the cataloguing instinct. The sheer number of tools is often taken as evidence of progress, yet the evidence reviewed here describes a field in which each new publication tends to add another integration method rather than consolidate best practice. Benchmarking studies of cancer subtype clustering [R4], multi-omics biomarker discovery [R50] and single-cell integration [R10, R37] each identify different top performers — SNF within colorectal cancer subtyping, DeePathNet and DeepKEGG in cancer biomarker discovery, and task-dependent leaders (totalVI, Seurat, MOJITOO, scAI, UINMF) for single-cell integration — indicating that method choice remains strongly context-dependent. The persistence of batch effects, platform-specific artefacts and the absence of agreed-upon reference datasets mean that methodological choice — not biological signal — frequently determines the headline result. Tool catalogues lengthen faster than standards mature, and the fragmentation that integration was meant to solve remains, in many respects, intact. The review that follows takes this tension as its starting point: it surveys the available software landscape across general-purpose frameworks, microbiome-centred tools, GUI platforms and containerised infrastructure, examines the limited but informative benchmarking evidence, and uses EasyMultiProfiler as a worked example of what a domain-specific, workflow-level solution can — and cannot — deliver relative to its alternatives.

General-purpose integration frameworks can be grouped along a continuum from tools that genuinely abstract the integration step—exposing it as a swappable component in a wider workflow—to packages that hard-wire a single algorithm and treat preprocessing or visualization as the only configurable layer. The most useful abstractions decouple three concerns: the data container, the integration operator, and the downstream statistical or biological interpretation. The R/Bioconductor ecosystem has been particularly fertile for this style of design. The moiraine package builds reproducible multi-omics pipelines that preprocess heterogeneous omics layers, dispatch them to one or more user-chosen integration methods, and return standardized outputs so that results can be compared across algorithms [R3]. Similarly, miodin offers a workflow-based syntax in which the same pipeline language supports vertical integration (same samples profiled on different platforms) and horizontal integration (same variables measured across studies), enabling transparent re-use of the same analysis scaffolding across transcriptomics, genomics and proteomics [R48]. timeOmics extends this philosophy to temporal designs—providing preprocessing, modeling and clustering of longitudinal multi-omics data and demonstrating it on the integrative Human Microbiome Project diabetes dataset combining mRNA, metabolites, gut taxa and clinical variables [R20]—while its companion netOmics builds hybrid multi-omics networks with smart node labeling and propagation to extract interpretable relationships from the same kind of data [R21]. These four packages share the property that the integration algorithm is an explicit, named object in the workflow: the user is not buying a single method but a methodology-neutral execution engine.

A second tier of R packages is method-centric yet generalizable, exposing a single integrative operator but with rich preprocessing, validation and visualization surrounding it. mixOmics and its supervised DIABLO extension [R27] form the canonical example, with reproducible workflows demonstrated for plant multi-omics under abiotic stress combining phenomics, metabolomics, proteomics and transcriptomics [R16]. CancerSubtypes packages four established subtype-identification algorithms behind a common interface, allowing feature selection, validation and biological follow-up to be swapped in and out [R49]. MUUMI sits between these tiers: it is presented as a unified R framework for statistical meta-analysis coupled with similarity network fusion and molecular interactome inference, but its integration layer is essentially fixed—the value-add is the coupling of meta-analysis to network interpretation rather than algorithm interchangeability [R2]. FindIT2 occupies a more specialized niche, providing a complete framework for TF target inference from ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq and RNA-seq that is highly generalizable across species but constrained to a single biological question [R45]. The Python side is currently less populated by neutral abstraction layers and more by deep-learning frameworks with fixed graph architectures, exemplified by BioNeuralNet, a modular graph neural network framework for end-to-end network-based multi-omics analysis [R5].

The benchmarking literature tempers expectations about the relative merit of these approaches. A large-scale study of 11 survival prediction methods across 18 TCGA multi-omics datasets found that methods explicitly accounting for multi-omics group structure performed only marginally better than naive single-block baselines, and only the block-forest variant—a tree-based ensemble that respects block boundaries—meaningfully outperformed a clinical Cox model [R46]. A benchmark of eight early, intermediate and late integration methods for colorectal cancer subtyping identified similarity network fusion (SNF) as the top performer across simulated and real-world datasets [R4]. A separate study benchmarking 20 statistical, machine-learning and deep-learning methods against gold-standard prognostic and therapeutic biomarkers ranked DeePathNet and DeepKEGG as top performers [R50]. The implication is sobering for the deep-learning community: statistical and machine-learning methods (boosting, penalized regression, random forest) implemented with a comparatively small methodological footprint remain competitive with far more elaborate architectures on tabular multi-omics data, and the additional complexity of graph attention, variational autoencoders or cycleGAN-based encoders is rarely justified by accuracy alone on cancer benchmarks.

Several limitations cut across this whole class of tools. First, the abstraction layers—moiraine, miodin, timeOmics—are R-centric, which makes them composable with the Bioconductor infrastructure (MultiAssayExperiment, SummarizedExperiment) but more difficult to weave into Python ecosystems that increasingly dominate deep-learning for omics. Second, the more specialized packages such as MUUMI, CancerSubtypes or the NMF-plus-metaheuristic framework combining adaptive gorilla troops optimization with sparse-joint NMF for cancer subtyping [R43] often lack head-to-head comparisons against the algorithms they are intended to complement, so claims of added value rest on demonstration rather than systematic benchmarking. Third, most frameworks are validated on a small number of case studies (IPF transcriptomes and THP-1 macrophages for MUUMI [R2]; Arabidopsis stress data for mixOmics [R16]; iHMP diabetes for timeOmics [R20]; TCGA glioblastoma and melanoma for the STATegra framework [R24]), which limits generalizability. The narrow evidence base and the absence of matched-condition head-to-head benchmarks across this entire class—including the Bioconductor-based microbiome workflows discussed later—mean that tool choice in practice rests on scope and infrastructure fit rather than demonstrated superiority on any standardized workload.

Microbiome research has long grappled with the gap between taxonomy-oriented surveys and functional understanding of microbial communities. The shift toward host–microbiome multi-omics—where metagenomics, metatranscriptomics, metaproteomics, metabolomics and host-response layers must be jointly analysed—exposes a sobering reality: most tools remain optimised for human cohorts and 16S-derived taxon profiles rather than for the cross-kingdom, functional, and non-model contexts in which microbiomes actually live. Aligning heterogeneous meta-omics layers with host molecular phenotypes remains the central unmet challenge that distinguishes microbiome-centred integration from generic cancer or single-cell pipelines, and the tools that address it remain unevenly distributed across the problems they claim to solve.

EasyMultiProfiler (EMP) is presented as a microbiome-focused workflow built on the SummarizedExperiment and MultiAssayExperiment data structures, organised into five interconnected modules—data extraction, preparation, support, analysis and visualisation—for standardised, reproducible multi-omics microbiome data integration [R1]. The motivation articulated in the EMP paper emphasises inconsistent sample coverage, heterogeneous data formats and complex analytical workflows as bottlenecks that erode reproducibility [R1]. In our reading, EMP's contribution lies in coordinating these steps within a coherent R-based workflow rather than introducing new integration mathematics; whether this coordination actually reduces methodological inconsistency between meta-omics datasets is a claim that would require benchmarking against equivalently curated pipelines and is not demonstrated in the cited work [R1]. The EMP publication does not document performance on non-model host-associated microbiomes, nor does it explicitly address whether the framework natively ingests cross-kingdom meta-omics layers alongside host omics [R1]. Practical dimensions such as explicit compositionality handling, missing-data policy and phylogeny-aware integration are not characterised in the available evidence either. The reader should therefore treat EMP as a documented R/Bioconductor option for host-microbiome multi-omics integration, not as a universal solution for cross-kingdom functional meta-omics.

gNOMO was built precisely for the underserved non-model case, integrating up to three meta-omics levels—metagenomics, metatranscriptomics and metaproteomics—through a Snakemake-managed pipeline demonstrated on the cockroach Blattella germanica gut microbiome [R26]. Its contribution is the explicit acknowledgement that sparse reference annotation is a key limitation when studying non-model organisms (exemplified by the invertebrate Blattella germanica), and that reproducibility tooling for such systems must be configurable and annotation-aware [R26]. Whether gNOMO natively incorporates host transcriptomics or metabolomics is not described in the available evidence; this is one practical gap that prospective users should evaluate against their own study designs. The contrast with EMP is therefore one of scope rather than methodological superiority: gNOMO targets raw meta-omics assembly for non-model hosts [R26], while EMP provides reproducible downstream integration on a Bioconductor data-class substrate [R1], and the two together sketch a fuller workflow than either alone.

CFViSA offers a web-based route, providing 79 analysis tools spanning sequence processing, visualisation and statistical analysis, combined with microbiome and transcriptome pipelines behind a unified interface [R40]. This lowers the barrier to entry for groups without dedicated bioinformatics capacity, but the platform is best characterised on current evidence as a statistical and visualisation suite; the upstream processing steps it actually performs are not specified in sufficient detail, so users requiring raw metagenomic read assembly or metapeptide identification should not assume coverage [R40]. As such, CFViSA complements rather than substitutes for dedicated meta-omics engines such as gNOMO's assembly pipeline [R26] or the upstream processing that EMP presupposes [R1].

The conceptual roadmaps proposed in recent reviews highlight precisely where these tools underperform. Perspective work on integrating multi-omics technologies to decipher microbiome functions emphasises standardised workflows, FAIR-compliant data objects, benchmarked datasets and community-driven initiatives as prerequisites for credible functional inference [R54], while translational reviews on inflammatory bowel disease argue that gut-microbiota-centred multi-omics must move beyond taxonomic dysbiosis signatures toward quantitative, longitudinally validated, action-linked biomarkers [R58]. Neither roadmap is operationally realised by the microbiome-centred tools examined here, and the available evidence does not establish whether any of them can recover known host–microbe mechanisms from integrated meta-omics in a head-to-head, community-accepted benchmark.

In sum, the microbiome-centred segment of the integration landscape is characterised by uneven coverage: EMP provides a reproducible Bioconductor workflow for host-microbiome multi-omics integration [R1], gNOMO pioneers non-model meta-omics reproducibility [R26], and CFViSA democratises downstream statistics [R40], but the field still over-relies on 16S-derived taxonomy, lacks a unified engine for functional meta-omics across kingdoms, and has no consensus benchmark for evaluating these workflows. The most consequential limitation across the board is that none of these tools has been benchmarked against the others on a shared, functionally annotated meta-omics testbed, leaving their relative accuracy largely an open question.
